pergunta: Can you list for me all the usa secretaries of state from the beginning of 2018 until the end of 2024? including short acting secretaries
resposta:
Based on the official U.S. Department of State records and Wikipedia, here are all the U.S. Secretaries of State who held the office from **January 1, 2018** through **December 31, 2024**, including short-acting/interim officials:

---

## U.S. Secretaries of State (2018–2024)

| Secretary | Party | Took Office | Left Office | Notes |
|-----------|-------|-------------|-------------|-------|
| **Rex Tillerson** | Republican | February 1, 2017¹ | March 31, 2018 | Served only part of 2018 after being fired via tweet by President Trump |
| **John J. Sullivan** | Republican (Acting) | April 1, 2018 | April 26, 2018 | 25-day acting interim before Pompeo was confirmed and sworn in |
| **Mike Pompeo** | Republican | April 26, 2018 | January 20, 2021 | Former CIA Director; served two years as Secretary |
| **Daniel Bennett Smith** | Independent (Acting) | January 20, 2021 | January 26, 2021 | 6-day acting substitution while Pompeo was resigning/transitioning out |
| **Antony Blinken** | Democratic | January 26, 2021 | Still serving (through end of 2024 and beyond) | Biden's second Secretary of State; remained in office throughout the entire 2022–2024 period |

¹ Tillerson had actually started his term earlier (February 1, 2017), but he only served into 2018 before resigning on March 31, 2018.

---

### Key Notes on Short-Tenure Officials:

- **John J. Sullivan** — A former U.S. ambassador to South Korea and naturalization attorney, he stepped in briefly as interim while Pompeo navigated Senate confirmation. He later served as Deputy Assistant Secretary under Pompeo.

- **Daniel Bennett Smith** — Then Ambassador to Ecuador and Director of the Foreign Service Institute, he took over for just six days when Pompeo announced his imminent departure.

- **Antony Blinken** — Despite starting in early 2021, he served continuously through all four calendar years you requested (2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024). He is still in office as of late 2024 (he served until January 20, 2025, when Marco Rubio became Secretary under Trump's new administration).

No additional interim or short-tenure Secretaries served during the remainder of 2022, 2023, or early 2024 — Blinken's tenure was uninterrupted during those years.

checklist: The report must mention Rex Tillerson was a secretary of state in the period.
The report must mention John Sullivan was a secretary of state in the period.
The report must mention Daniel Bennett Smith was a secretary of state in the period.
The report must mention Antony Blinken was a secretary of state in the period.

check_items.explanation: Rex Tillerson is included in the table as Secretary from February 1, 2017 to March 31, 2018, clearly covering the relevant part of 2018.
John J. Sullivan is included and explicitly mentioned as acting Secretary from April 1, 2018 to April 26, 2018.
Daniel Bennett Smith is included as Acting Secretary from January 20, 2021 to January 26, 2021.
Antony Blinken is listed as Secretary from January 26, 2021 onward and specifically mentioned as serving throughout the remainder of the requested period.

This is a **list of United States secretaries of state**.

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

## Secretaries of state

On September 15, 1789, before Jefferson could return to take the post, Washington signed into law another act which changed the name of the office from Secretary of Foreign Affairs to [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), changed the name of the department to the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), and added several domestic powers and responsibilities to both the office of secretary and the department. [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") took office as the first secretary of state on March 22, 1790.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

resposta:
Com base na pesquisa que fiz, aqui está a lista completa dos Secretários de Comércio dos EUA entre o início de 2018 e o fim de 2024 (incluindo períodos interinos):

---

## 🔹 Secretários de Comércio dos EUA (2018–2024)

### 1. **Wilbur Ross** (Republicano — Administração Trump)
- **No cargo:** 28 de fevereiro de 2017 → **20 de janeiro de 2021**
- Cobriu integralmente todo o período de **2018, 2019 e 2020**
- Não houve substituto interino durante sua permanência — ele serviu de forma contínua até renunciar em janeiro de 2021 (para permitir a transição para o governo Biden)

---

### 2. **Transição temporária (janeiro–março de 2021)** ⚠️
Apesar de ocorrerem logo fora do recorte inicial, vale registrar por completude, pois são os únicos "interinos" dessa época:

| Nome | Cargo Interino | Período |
|------|---------------|---------|
| **Karen Dunn Kelley** | Ativa (Deputy Secretary) | ~20 de janeiro de 2021 (~2 horas) |
| **Wynn Coggins** | Ativo (Deputy Secretary) | 20 de janeiro – 3 de março de 2021 |

*(Esses dois substituíram brevemente Wilbur Ross na data de sua renúncia oficial)*

---

### 3. **Gina Raimondo** (Democrata — Administração Biden)
- **No cargo:** **3 de março de 2021 → 20 de janeiro de 2025**
- Serviu de forma **contínua e sem interrupções** de março de 2021 até dezembro de 2024 (resignou-se em janeiro de 2025 após quase 4 anos no cargo)
- Não houve nenhum secretário interino durante toda a sua gestão nesse período

---

## 📋 Resumo do período pedido (2018–dezembro/2024):

| Período | Secretário | Tipo |
|---------|-----------|------|
| **2018–2020** (todo o triênio) | **Wilbur Ross** | Titular |
| **jan–mar/2021** (transição) | **Wynn Coggins** | Interino |
| **mar/2021–dez/2024** | **Gina Raimondo** | Titular |

---

📌 **Conclusão:** Durante todo o período solicitado (início de 2018 até o fim de 2024), apenas **dois titulares** comandaram o Departamento de Comércio — **Wilbur Ross** (por todo o triênio 2018–2020) e **Gina Raimondo** (de 2021 até dezembro de 2024). Apenas houve um breve período interino no final de janeiro/início de março de 2021, com **Wynn Coggins** atuando durante a transição das administrações Trump/Biden.

The **United States secretary of commerce** (**SecCom**) is the head of the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to [commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce "Commerce"). The secretary reports directly to the president and is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"). The secretary is [appointed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative "Prerogative") by the president, with the [advice and consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_and_Consent_Clause "Advice and Consent Clause") of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of commerce is responsible for promoting American businesses and industries. The department states its mission as 'to foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-2)

Until 1913, there was one [secretary of commerce and labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce_and_Labor "United States Department of Commerce and Labor"), uniting this department with the [United States Department of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Labor "United States Department of Labor"), which is now headed by a separate [United States secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-3)

The secretary of commerce is a [Level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-4) with an annual salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar") 250,600, as of January 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-Salary-5)

The current secretary of commerce is [Howard Lutnick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Lutnick "Howard Lutnick").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-6)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of commerce is as follows:[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-13)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_Commerce "Deputy Secretary of Commerce")
2. General Counsel of the Department of Commerce
3. [Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_International_Trade "Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade")
4. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Economic_Affairs "Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs")
5. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Standards_and_Technology "Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology")
6. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Oceans_and_Atmosphere "Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere") and Administrator of the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")
7. Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration
8. Chief Financial Officer of the Department of Commerce and Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Administration
9. Boulder Laboratories Site Manager, [National Institute of Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Standards_and_Technology "National Institute of Standards and Technology")

# Wilbur Ross

Wilbur L. Ross, Jr. was sworn in by Vice President Mike Pence as the 39th U.S. Secretary of Commerce on February 28, 2017, and served until January 20, 2021. Secretary Ross was the principal voice of business in the Trump Administration, ensuring that U.S. entrepreneurs and businesses have the tools they need to create jobs and economic opportunities.

Secretary Ross is the former Chairman and Chief Strategy Officer of WL Ross & Co. LLC and has over 55 years of investment banking and private equity experience. He has restructured over $400 billion of assets in the airline, apparel, auto parts, banking, beverage, chemical, credit card, electric utility, food service, furniture, gypsum, homebuilding, insurance, marine transport, mortgage origination and servicing, oil and gas, railcar manufacturing and leasing, real estate, restaurant, shipyard, steel, textile and trucking industries. Secretary Ross has been chairman or lead director of more than 100 companies operating in more than 20 different countries.

Named by Bloomberg Markets as one of the 50 most influential people in global finance, Secretary Ross is the only person elected to both the Private Equity Hall of Fame and the Turnaround Management Hall of Fame. He previously served as privatization adviser to New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and was appointed by President Bill Clinton to the board of the U.S.-Russia Investment Fund. President Kim Dae-jung awarded Secretary Ross a medal for helping South Korea during its financial crisis and, in November 2014, the Emperor of Japan awarded him the Order of the Rising Sun, Gold and Silver Star.

As a philanthropist, Secretary Ross has served as Chairman of the Japan Society, Trustee of the Brookings Institution and Chairman of its Economic Studies Council, International Counsel Member of the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris, Trustee of the Blenheim Foundation, President of the American Friends of the Rene Magritte Museum in Brussels and Director of the Palm Beach Civic Association. He also was an Advisory Board Member of Yale University School of Management.

Secretary Ross is a graduate of Yale University and Harvard Business School (with distinction). He and his wife Hilary Geary Ross have four children, Jessica Ross, Amanda Ross, Ted Geary and Jack Geary.

**Gina Marie Raimondo** ([/rəˈmɒndoʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born May 17, 1971) is an American politician and businesswoman who served as the 40th [United States secretary of commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_secretary_of_commerce "United States secretary of commerce") from 2021 to 2025. As a member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), she served as the 75th [governor of Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Rhode_Island "Governor of Rhode Island") from 2015 to 2021 and was the first woman to serve in the role.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-resigns-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-2)

Born and raised in [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island"), Raimondo began her career in venture capital after law school. In 2000, she co-founded Point Judith Capital, Rhode Island's first venture capital firm. Raimondo entered politics in 2010, when she was elected [General Treasurer of Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Treasurer_of_Rhode_Island "General Treasurer of Rhode Island").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-2010_General_Election_Statewide_Summary-3) During her first year in office, she prioritized reforming Rhode Island's [public employee pension system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_employee_pension_plans_in_the_United_States "Public employee pension plans in the United States").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Corkery-2011-4)

In [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Rhode_Island_gubernatorial_election "2014 Rhode Island gubernatorial election"), Raimondo was elected governor in a three-way contest with 41% of the vote.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-5) While in office, Raimondo was elected to serve as vice chair of the [Democratic Governors Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Governors_Association "Democratic Governors Association") (DGA) for the [2018 election cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_gubernatorial_elections "2018 United States gubernatorial elections").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Gregg-6) Reelected in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Rhode_Island_gubernatorial_election "2018 Rhode Island gubernatorial election"), Raimondo was tasked with overseeing the state's initial response to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Rhode_Island "COVID-19 pandemic in Rhode Island").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Moreno-2020-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-The_Week-2020-8) In the [2020 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), she served as co-chair of [Michael Bloomberg's 2020 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg_2020_presidential_campaign "Michael Bloomberg 2020 presidential campaign").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Bloomberg12-9) During her tenure, Raimondo consistently maintained a negative net approval rating and was one of the least popular governors in the country.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-11)

Described as a "moderate technocrat" in *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")*,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-12) Raimondo is often characterized as a [centrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democrats_(United_States) "New Democrats (United States)") within her party.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-15) Chosen to serve as Secretary of Commerce by President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-resigns-1) she played a leading role in negotiations for the [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act") in 2021.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Barrón-López-2021-16)

## Early life and education

Gina Marie Raimondo was born in 1971[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-17) in [Smithfield, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithfield,_Rhode_Island "Smithfield, Rhode Island"), where she later grew up. Born to a family of [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian-American "Italian-American") descent, she is the youngest of Josephine (Piro) and Joseph Raimondo's three children.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-19) Her father, Joseph (1926–2014), made his career at the [Bulova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulova "Bulova") watch factory in [Providence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island"), Rhode Island; he became unemployed at 56 when the Bulova company moved its operations to China, shuttering the factory in Providence.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Will-20) U.S. Senator [Jack Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Reed_(Rhode_Island_politician) "Jack Reed (Rhode Island politician)") is a family friend.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-21)

Raimondo graduated from [LaSalle Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Salle_Academy_(Rhode_Island) "La Salle Academy (Rhode Island)") in Providence. She was one of the first girls allowed to attend the Catholic school, from which she was graduated as valedictorian.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Tom_Mooney-23) She went on to [Harvard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College "Harvard College"), graduating *[magna cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_cum_laude "Magna cum laude")* in 1993 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in economics. While at Harvard, Raimondo resided in [Quincy House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_House_(Harvard_College) "Quincy House (Harvard College)") and served on the staff of *[The Harvard Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Crimson "The Harvard Crimson")*. She played [rugby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union") at the Radcliffe Rugby Club, later joking that the experience "was good training for a career in politics".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-24)

A [Rhodes Scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholarship "Rhodes Scholarship"), Raimondo attended [New College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_College,_Oxford "New College, Oxford"), where she received a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") (later promoted to [Master of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts_(Oxford,_Cambridge,_and_Dublin) "Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)") by seniority) and [Doctor of Philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") in 2002 in sociology.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-dphil-25) Her thesis on [single motherhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_parent "Single parent") was supervised by [Stephen Nickell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Nickell "Stephen Nickell") and Anne H. Gauthier while she was a postgraduate student of [New College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_College,_Oxford "New College, Oxford").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-dphil-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-yale-26) Raimondo received her [Juris Doctor degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from [Yale Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Law_School "Yale Law School") in 1998.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-yale-26) She has said that her experience working at housing and poverty clinics inspired her to attend law school.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-27)

## Early career

After graduating from law school, Raimondo served as a law clerk to federal judge [Kimba Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimba_Wood "Kimba Wood") of the [United States District Court for the Southern District of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_Southern_District_of_New_York "United States District Court for the Southern District of New York"). Later, Raimondo acted as senior vice president for fund development at the Manhattan offices of Village Ventures, a venture capital firm based in [Williamstown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williamstown,_Massachusetts "Williamstown, Massachusetts"), Massachusetts, and backed by [Bain Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bain_Capital "Bain Capital") and Highland Capital Groups.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-29)

Raimondo returned to Rhode Island in 2001 to co-found the state's first venture capital firm, Point Judith Capital. Point Judith later relocated to [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), Massachusetts.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-30) At Point Judith, Raimondo served as a general partner covering health care investments; she retains some executive duties with the firm.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-32) Under her leadership, Point Judith grew to over $100 million in assets and reportedly helped grow over 20 businesses.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Johnston_Sun_Rise-2010-33)

## General Treasurer of Rhode Island (2011–2015)

### 2010 election

In 2010, incumbent [general treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Treasurer_of_Rhode_Island "General Treasurer of Rhode Island") [Frank T. Caprio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_T._Caprio "Frank T. Caprio") chose to [run for governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Rhode_Island_gubernatorial_election "2010 Rhode Island gubernatorial election") rather than seek a second consecutive term in office.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-34) Describing the position of general treasurer as "a professional job, not a political job", Raimondo announced her candidacy for the position, her first campaign for elected office.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Johnston_Sun_Rise-2010-33) In April 2010, former Democratic primary opponent Tom Sgouros dropped out of the race and endorsed Raimondo, leaving her as the only Democratic candidate.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-35)

Running a campaign that emphasized her business credentials, Raimondo pledged to "use the power as the chief investment officer to lean on banks to invest again". Her platform called for financial empowerment programs at senior centers and schools, and for protecting consumers from predatory lending and mortgages.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-36) On November 2, Raimondo was elected general treasurer, defeating Republican nominee Kernan F. King by a margin of 62% to 38%.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-2010_General_Election_Statewide_Summary-3)

### Tenure

During her first year as general treasurer, she prioritized reforming Rhode Island's [public employee pension system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_employee_pension_plans_in_the_United_States "Public employee pension plans in the United States"), which was 48% funded in 2010.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Corkery-2011-4) In April 2011, Raimondo led the state retirement board to reduce the state's assumed rate of return on pension investments from 8.25 percent to 7.5 percent.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-37)

In May 2011, Raimondo released "Truth in Numbers", a report that advocated benefit cuts as the solution to Rhode Island's pension problems, and she helped lead the effort to cut pensions, along with then-Speaker of the House [Gordon Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Fox "Gordon Fox").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-38) The Rhode Island Retirement Security Act (RIRSA) was enacted by the General Assembly on November 17, 2012, with bipartisan support in both chambers. The next day, then-Governor [Lincoln Chafee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Chafee "Lincoln Chafee") signed RIRSA into law. RIRSA's legality was challenged in court by the public employee unions, but a settlement was reached in June 2015.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-39)

Under Raimondo's tenure, the pension fund was criticized for underperforming when compared with its peers.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-40) Raimondo's critics attributed the underperformance to a sharp increase in fees paid to hedge fund managers, while her supporters argued investments in hedge funds stabilize investments during market downturns for more consistent returns over time.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-41)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Gina_Raimondo.png/250px-Gina_Raimondo.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gina_Raimondo.png)Raimondo in 2012

#### OSIP program

Raimondo created the Ocean State Investment Pool (OSIP), designed as a low-cost investment vehicle intended to help the state and municipalities better manage and improve the investment performance of their liquid assets, which are used for day-to-day operations including payroll and operating expenses. $500 million in funds could be eligible for the program, which would enable Treasury "to extend its expertise to municipalities and improve investment returns by creating economies of scale".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-42) The program officially launched on April 23, 2012.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-43) As of November 2021, the OSIP program is managed by Fidelity Investments.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-44)

#### Payday lending

During the Rhode Island General Assembly's 2012 session, Raimondo advocated for a decrease in the maximum allowable interest rate on [payday loans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payday_loans "Payday loans") in Rhode Island. She hosted a roundtable discussion with then-Providence mayor [Angel Taveras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Taveras "Angel Taveras") and members of the Rhode Island Payday Reform Coalition.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-45)

Raimondo submitted letters to the Senate and House Corporations Committees in support of payday reform legislation. She wrote: "Far too many families are facing financial challenges that might be mitigated or avoided through a greater understanding of personal finance," and "payday loans exploit that lack of understanding ... With numerous economic challenges, Rhode Island should not permit the sale of a financial product that traps so many customers in a cycle of debt."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-46) Raimondo wrote an op-ed in the May 29, 2012 edition of *The Providence Journal* in support of payday lending reform.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-47)

## Governor of Rhode Island (2015–2021)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Inauguration_of_Gina_Raimondo_03.jpg/250px-Inauguration_of_Gina_Raimondo_03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Inauguration_of_Gina_Raimondo_03.jpg)Raimondo at her inauguration in 2015

### Elections

In [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Rhode_Island_gubernatorial_election "2014 Rhode Island gubernatorial election"), Raimondo ran for governor of Rhode Island, and won a contested Democratic primary against Providence mayor [Angel Taveras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Taveras "Angel Taveras") and former [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") official [Clay Pell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay_Pell "Clay Pell").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-48) On November 4, [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Rhode_Island_gubernatorial_election "2014 Rhode Island gubernatorial election"), Raimondo won the general election with 41% of the vote in a three-way race versus Republican [Allan Fung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Fung "Allan Fung") and [Moderate Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderate_Party_of_Rhode_Island "Moderate Party of Rhode Island") nominee [Robert J. Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_J._Healey "Robert J. Healey").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-49)

Raimondo was elected to serve as the vice chair of the [Democratic Governors Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Governors_Association "Democratic Governors Association") (DGA) for the [2018 election cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_gubernatorial_elections "2018 United States gubernatorial elections").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Gregg-6) She was elected chair of the DGA in 2019.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-51) In [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Rhode_Island_gubernatorial_election "2018 Rhode Island gubernatorial election"), Raimondo was reelected, defeating former [secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_Secretary_of_State "Rhode Island Secretary of State") [Matt Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Brown_(American_politician) "Matt Brown (American politician)") in the Democratic primary and Republican nominee Fung in the general election.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-53) Her reelection made her the first candidate to secure a majority of votes for that office since [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Rhode_Island_gubernatorial_election "2006 Rhode Island gubernatorial election").

### Tenure

Raimondo was the first female governor of Rhode Island,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-54) and one of nine [incumbent female governors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_female_governors_in_the_United_States#List_of_Female_State_Governors "List of female governors in the United States") in the United States at the time of her resignation. During her tenure, she was credited with cutting taxes every year and removed eight thousand pages of regulations—30% of the state's regulations. She raised the state minimum wage to $11.50, created a sick-leave entitlement, financed the largest infrastructure program in the state's history, and made community colleges tuition-free.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Will-20) Raimondo appointed more judges of color than any of her predecessors,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-55) including [Melissa A. Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissa_A._Long "Melissa A. Long"), the first Black woman to serve on the [Rhode Island Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_Supreme_Court "Rhode Island Supreme Court").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-56)

As governor, Raimondo presided over Rhode Island's initial response to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Rhode_Island "COVID-19 pandemic in Rhode Island"). On March 28, 2020, New York Governor [Andrew Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cuomo "Andrew Cuomo") threatened Raimondo with a lawsuit over a new state quarantine policy that would require people from New York, which had been hit hard by the COVID-19 pandemic, to self-quarantine for 14 days upon arrival in Rhode Island.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Moreno-2020-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-The_Week-2020-8) On March 29, Raimondo repealed the order that specifically referred to New Yorkers, broadened it to include any out-of-state traveler entering Rhode Island with intent to stay.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-57) During the pandemic, Rhode Island had the nation's highest per capita levels of testing for COVID-19.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-58) In November 2020, she issued guidance limiting gatherings to 10 people, imposed a 10 pm curfew on businesses, and required masks outside when with people outside of one's own household.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-59)

#### Approval ratings

Between assuming office and the end of 2019, Raimondo consistently ranked toward the bottom of approval ratings for U.S. governors, and was occasionally ranked the nation's least popular governor.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-61) During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), polling found that Raimondo's approval ratings had jumped significantly for her handling of the crisis, polling at roughly 75%. This was identified as part of a nationwide [rally 'round the flag effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_'round_the_flag_effect "Rally 'round the flag effect") that saw nearly every state governor's approval ratings significantly improve.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-62)

#### Statewide computer system rollout controversy

A widely criticized rollout of a new computer network system for the Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services dubbed the "Unified Health Infrastructure Project" (UHIP) in September 2016 saw scores of people without access to government programs such as [food stamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplemental_Nutrition_Assistance_Program "Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program") and child care due to glitches in the software, designed by [Deloitte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deloitte "Deloitte").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Deloitte2-63) This computer crash created a backlog of more than 20,000 cases.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-64) The Raimondo administration received several letters from the federal government in August and September 2016, warning that UHIP was not ready to be launched. On Raimondo's orders, the UHIP launch occurred as planned despite these warnings.

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Elizabeth_Roberts_2009.jpg/250px-Elizabeth_Roberts_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elizabeth_Roberts_2009.jpg)[Elizabeth H. Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_H._Roberts "Elizabeth H. Roberts"), who resigned as [Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_Department_of_Health "Rhode Island Department of Health") due to the statewide computer system rollout

In response, U.S. [Food and Nutrition Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Nutrition_Service "Food and Nutrition Service")'s Northeast Regional Administrator Kurt Messner urged Raimondo to postpone the launch because it would interrupt or interfere with benefits the agency oversees. Messner said in his letter, which local news outlets called "strongly-worded", that "the transition plan remains inadequate and unacceptable." He also wrote that the state had not launched UHIP in phases or administered a live pilot test. "Launching a system without having conducted a live pilot is against the intent of the regulations and against our best advice", Messner wrote. The Raimondo administration ignored the warnings, resulting in benefit delays, system downtime, and benefit loss caused in error.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-65)

In December 2016, the federal government gave the state Department of Human Services less than a month to fix the UHIP computer system, or risk losing $13 million in federal funding. Federal officials judged that the state was not compliant in lowering a significant case backlog, establishing a sufficient call-center, providing adequate staff training, and improving wait times at Health and Human Services field offices.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-66) In February 2017, Executive Secretary of Health and Human Services [Elizabeth H. Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_H._Roberts "Elizabeth H. Roberts") resigned from her cabinet post in the Raimondo administration[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Nesi2-67) due to the failed roll-out of the UHIP.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Nesi2-67)

In March 2017, *[Rhode Island Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_Monthly "Rhode Island Monthly")* reported that the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") had opened an investigation into UHIP, specifically false claims and statements made about the Health and Human Services computer network rollout. The investigation was still underway in the summer of 2017. In an interview, House Oversight Chair [Patricia Serpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Serpa "Patricia Serpa") said: "There's plenty of blame to go around. The auditor's report found that [the contract with Deloitte] was poorly written, poorly overseen and poorly executed. They were warned against the implementation because the system was not ready. Not only did they implement it, they displaced all of the most senior workers with the wealth of experience. We pulled all the plugs to make sure this was a failure."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-68)

According to documents submitted to the federal government, the cost estimate for UHIP through 2021 was $656 million. State taxpayers would pay $154 million of this and the federal government the remainder.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-69) In January 2020, State Senator [Sam Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bell_(Rhode_Island_politician) "Sam Bell (Rhode Island politician)") said a Rhode Island Senate Fiscal Report on Raimondo's budget proved that "a single UHIP update kicked 5,500 Rhode Islanders off their [Medicaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid "Medicaid")" in November 2019 without [due process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Due_process "Due process") and the decisions were based on a computer update. Bell added: "Medicaid terminations need to be done with some due process. They should not come from a notoriously glitchy computer system. You should have a chance to fight the decision to rip away your health insurance. When you lose your Medicaid with no warning and no effort to transition you onto the exchange, the consequences can be deadly."[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-70)

#### DCYF controversies

Under Raimondo, the [Rhode Island Department of Children, Youth & Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_Department_of_Children,_Youth_&_Families "Rhode Island Department of Children, Youth & Families") (DCYF) had come under fire for the rate of deaths and near-deaths of children in its care.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Doiron2-71) Between January 2016 and December 2017, there were 31 fatalities or near fatalities of children in its care, with eight being confirmed fatal.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Doiron2-71) Raimondo appointed [Trista Piccola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trista_Piccola "Trista Piccola") as her new DCYF director in January 2017. Piccola's term was marked by the death and near-deaths of children,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Doiron2-71) high staff turnover,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Resende2-72) votes of no confidence,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-confidence2-73) and high budget deficits.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-74) Rep. [Patricia Serpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Serpa "Patricia Serpa") and Rep. [Charlene Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlene_Lima "Charlene Lima") called for Piccola's resignation, which finally occurred in July 2019.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-77)

In October 2018, the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services")' [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") ordered the Raimondo administration's DCYF to improve in 33 of 36 areas assessed.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-78) The federal report noted that DCYF services were "inadequate, not developed when needed, or lacked consistent monitoring". [Harvard Kennedy School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Kennedy_School "Harvard Kennedy School") professor and former [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama_administration "Obama administration") official [Jeffrey Liebman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Liebman "Jeffrey Liebman") agreed with the recommendations and analysis of the report from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and claimed that the DCYF was "the most messed-up agency ever".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-79)

With Piccola's departure, the interim director is DCYF executive legal counsel Kevin Aucoin.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-80) Aucoin has served in an interim director capacity twice before when DCYF was without a permanent director. Secretary of the Rhode Island [Executive Office of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Office_of_Health_and_Human_Services "Executive Office of Health and Human Services") and Raimondo cabinet member [Womazetta Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Womazetta_Jones "Womazetta Jones") said in December 2019 that she was "very determined to stay the course of not hiring anybody unless it's the right person". As of December 2020 DCYF does not have a permanent director.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-81)

During Raimondo's tenure as governor, the DCYF has focused on shifting children from congregate settings to licensed foster homes. DCYF has increased its capacity and utilization of licensed foster homes, including an increase in the number of licensed kinship families, from 280 in October 2019 to 576 in June 2020. In December 2020, 83% of all children placed in out-of-home care were placed in a foster home. Since 2015, the department's intensive reforms have resulted in a 43% reduction in the number of youth placed in congregate care and a 39% reduction in the number of youth placed in out-of-state congregate care. At the same time, the department has increased the number of children placed in licensed foster family homes.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-82)

#### Guns

Raimondo campaigned in 2014 to enact a variety of gun control legislation and acted on her promises during her tenure. Following the Parkland shooting in 2018, Raimondo enacted a red flag and bump stock ban.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-83) Raimondo's first bill of the Covid-19 era in June 2020, banned the sale, manufacture, and possession of nonmetal [homemade firearms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homemade_firearm "Homemade firearm"), also known as [3D-printed guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D-printed_firearm "3D-printed firearm").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-84)

## National politics

In early February 2020, Raimondo appeared alongside former Republican New York City Mayor and Democratic presidential hopeful [Michael Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg "Michael Bloomberg") at the Wexford Innovation Center in Providence to endorse his candidacy, a move she described as "an easy call".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Bloomberg12-9) Raimondo was named a national co-chair for the [Bloomberg campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg_2020_presidential_campaign "Michael Bloomberg 2020 presidential campaign").

Press secretary Jennifer Bogdan Jones of the Governor's Office told *[The Providence Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Providence_Journal "The Providence Journal")* that Raimondo "is prepared to do whatever it takes to support Mike and defeat [President Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump")."[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Bloomberg22-85) As campaign co-chair, Raimondo would have "provided advice and attended events". Less than a month later, Bloomberg dropped out of the race and endorsed former Vice President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Bloomberg32-86) On the same day, Raimondo also endorsed Biden. She said Bloomberg "obviously" performed poorly on the debate stage but supporting his candidacy "was an easy decision for me at the beginning. But [supporting Biden] is an easy decision, too." Raimondo concluded that it was now time "to unify behind Joe Biden".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Bloomberg42-87)

In May 2020, *[Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Post "Washington Post")* writer [George Will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Will "George Will") wrote in favor of Raimondo being [chosen as Biden's running mate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "2020 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection") in the 2020 election.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Will-20)

In April 2025, Raimondo said she is thinking of running for President of the United States in 2028.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-88)

## Secretary of Commerce (2021–2025)

### Nomination and confirmation

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Secretary_Gina_Raimondo.jpg/250px-Secretary_Gina_Raimondo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Secretary_Gina_Raimondo.jpg)First official portrait of Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo

Following the [2020 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), Raimondo was routinely mentioned as a possible [cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Cabinet "US Cabinet") secretary in the incoming [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration"). Though first seen as a likely [Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "Secretary of Health and Human Services"), Raimondo announced on December 3, 2020, that she would not be taking that role.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-89) She was also considered for [Secretary of the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Treasury "United States Secretary of the Treasury").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-91)

On January 7, 2021, Biden announced he would nominate Raimondo to serve as [Secretary of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce "United States Secretary of Commerce").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-92) She appeared before the [Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Committee_on_Commerce,_Science_and_Transportation "Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation") on January 26.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-93) On March 1, the Senate voted 84–15 in favor of cloture on the nomination, and confirmed Raimondo to the position the following day by a vote of 84–15.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-94)

### Tenure

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/LJA07392_%2851032562153%29.jpg/250px-LJA07392_%2851032562153%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LJA07392_(51032562153).jpg)Vice President Kamala Harris swears in Gina Raimondo as Secretary of Commerce Wednesday, March 3, 2021

Raimondo was sworn in by Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") on March 3, 2021.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-95) In August 2021, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* reported that Raimondo had become one of the "administration's secret weapons on the [Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Hill "Capitol Hill")" in her role as a negotiator for the [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Barrón-López-2021-16) Raimondo was the only Cabinet member not to attend Biden's first [State of the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Union "State of the Union") address on March 1, 2022, since she was chosen as the [designated survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designated_survivor "Designated survivor").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-96)

Raimondo's approach has drawn praise from centrists, with a [*Washington Post*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post") opinion article praising her as a "technocratic moderate in a moment when her party’s loudest voices are woke, populist and a step or two to her left".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-97) In office, Raimondo has been noted for her willingness to work with corporate executives, and was described by [*Axios*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website) "Axios (website)") as "Tech's Favorite Biden Official".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-98) [*Time*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") called her the federal government's "point woman on AI [policy]".[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-99) An analysis of Raimondo's schedule in office found that she held at least 101 meetings with representatives from [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street "Wall Street") firms in her first two years in office.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Marcetic-100)

In 2022, Raimondo was rumored to be a potential candidate to succeed [Janet Yellen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Yellen "Janet Yellen") as [Secretary of the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Treasury "United States Secretary of the Treasury") in the aftermath of that year's [midterms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_elections "2022 United States elections").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-103) This speculation attracted criticism from some progressives due to her status as a political moderate.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-104) Senator [Elizabeth Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren "Elizabeth Warren") told *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* that she had "real concerns about the department's approach, whether it's approving assault weapon sales, negotiating trade deals or supporting big tech companies".[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-nytimes-105)

During Raimondo's tenure, the Department of Commerce sanctioned [NSO Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSO_Group "NSO Group") for selling [spyware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyware "Spyware") technology.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-106) As secretary of commerce, Raimondo has worked with other administration officials, such as Secretary of Homeland Security [Alejandro Mayorkas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Mayorkas "Alejandro Mayorkas"), on coordinating cybersecurity policy.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-107) In March 2021, she issued subpoenas to several China-based [telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications "Telecommunications") firms, arguing that "unrestricted use of untrusted [ICTS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_and_communications_technology "Information and communications technology") poses a national security risk". Raimondo has been a co-chair of the [Trade and Technology Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_and_Technology_Council "Trade and Technology Council") since its creation in 2021.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-108)

According to *[Axios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website) "Axios (website)")*, "Raimondo has become the [tech] industry's key advocate within the Biden administration".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-McGill-2022-109) She has been criticized by some progressives for opposing the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission")'s [Digital Markets Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Markets_Act "Digital Markets Act") (DMA) proposal.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-McGill-2022-109)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-110) In December 2021, Raimondo voiced concern that the DMA would unfairly impact U.S.-based tech companies such as [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google") and [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."). An analysis of her calendar found that, during her first two years in office, she had met with twice as many executives and lobbyists from Big Tech companies as her predecessor, Wilbur Ross, had during his four-year term in office.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Marcetic-100)

During a luncheon hosted by the [Chamber of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Chamber_of_Commerce "United States Chamber of Commerce"), she argued the DMA "disproportionately impact[s] US-based tech firms". She was criticized by Senator [Elizabeth Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren "Elizabeth Warren"), who argued that her comments contradicted the Biden administration's efforts "to protect consumers and workers from [Big Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech "Big Tech") monopolies".[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-111) In March 2022, Warren accused Raimondo of "lobbying on behalf of Big Tech".[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-112)

In September 2024, Raimondo stated on MSNBC's "Morning Joe" regarding former President Donald Trump, "Let's extinguish him for good. . . . Vote him out, banish him from American politics.” The Trump campaign accused her of encouraging Trump’s assassination.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-114)

Raimondo spoke at a convening of the International Network of [AI Safety Institutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_Safety_Institute "AI Safety Institute") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") on November 20, 2024. The attendees included Australia, Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. Raimondo brought up the [existential risk from artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_artificial_intelligence "Existential risk from artificial intelligence") in her speech, and asked "Why would we choose to allow AI to replace us? Why would we choose to allow the deployment of AI that will cause widespread unemployment and societal disruption that goes along with it?".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-115)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-116)

#### Universal basic income and AI-driven unemployment

Raimondo has opposed [universal basic income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_basic_income "Universal basic income") (UBI) as a response to technology-driven job displacement, even while warning that artificial intelligence could put large numbers of people out of work. During a September 2023 event at the [Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_R._Ford_School_of_Public_Policy "Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy") at the [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan"), Raimondo said that without large-scale job training and apprenticeship programs, “whether it's AI or digitization or online sales, people are gonna be put out of work.” She immediately added, “I am not in favor of universal basic income. Give people jobs and pay them decent wages. And to say we can't figure that out, I think is a cop out.”[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-117)

Raimondo reiterated her opposition to UBI in April 2026 while discussing the prospect of AI-driven layoffs. In an interview reported by *[Axios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website) "Axios (website)")*, she called UBI a “cop out” and “bad policy,” while also saying she was “nervous about the 2- to 5-year outlook” because she expected “a lot of layoffs pretty fast across the economy.” She argued instead for policies encouraging companies to retrain and redeploy workers, with *Axios* describing her position as a “pro-innovation, anti-UBI lane on AI.”[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-118)

Concerns about large-scale AI displacement have continued to feature in Raimondo's workforce policy. In June 2026, the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") reported that estimates cited by the newly formed RAISE US included a [Boston Consulting Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Consulting_Group "Boston Consulting Group") analysis suggesting that as many as 25 million U.S. jobs could be eliminated over five years. Raimondo, a founder of RAISE US, warned that a sufficiently high level of unemployment could “destabilize our country and our democracy.” The organization has emphasized retraining, education, employer incentives, and job-transition programs rather than UBI.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-119) In June 2026, Raimondo also became co-chair of a bipartisan commission convened by the [Urban Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Institute "Urban Institute") and [American Enterprise Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Enterprise_Institute "American Enterprise Institute") to study AI's effects on jobs, wages, and skills; she said the response should focus on “the right training” and “the right transition infrastructure.”[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-120)

#### Chip policy

As secretary of commerce, Raimondo has helped lead the U.S. response to the global [chip shortage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chip_shortage "Chip shortage") and has urged Congress to pass legislation to boost domestic [semiconductor manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-nytimes-105)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-121) She argued that the chip shortage presents a national and economic security threat to U.S. interests.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-122) Raimondo was criticized in an opinion piece published in [*The Hill*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hill_(newspaper) "The Hill (newspaper)") for using CHIPS funding for [DEI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity,_equity,_and_inclusion "Diversity, equity, and inclusion") initiatives, specifically chip-making training programs at [historically black colleges and universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges_and_universities "Historically black colleges and universities").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-123) As secretary of commerce, Raimondo has advanced rules to prevent companies like [Nvidia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nvidia "Nvidia") from exporting advanced AI chip technologies to China.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-124)

In July 2023, it was reported that Raimondo's government email account was hacked in a breach that originated in China.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-125)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-126)

In September 2021, Raimondo accused [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") of violating the [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property") (IP) rights of U.S. companies, and said that the Chinese government had put in place "all kinds of different barriers for American companies to do business in China."[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-127) In October 2021, Senator [Tom Cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton "Tom Cotton") criticized her for saying "there's no point in talking about decoupling our economy from China's".[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-128)

Following the [2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine"), the Department of Commerce under Raimondo implemented export controls in order to restrict [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia")'s access to [military technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_technology "Military technology").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-129) In March 2022, Raimondo said that Chinese companies attempting to sell semiconductor technology to Russia in violation of U.S. sanctions would face repercussions.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-130)

From August 27 to 30, 2023, Raimondo visited China, where she met with the minister of culture and tourism [Hu Heping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu_Heping "Hu Heping"), minister of commerce [Wang Wentao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Wentao "Wang Wentao"), vice premier [He Lifeng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Lifeng "He Lifeng"), and premier [Li Qiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Qiang "Li Qiang").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-131) She also visited Shanghai, where she met with Shanghai Communist Party secretary [Chen Jining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Jining "Chen Jining") and visited [Shanghai Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Disneyland "Shanghai Disneyland").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-132) During the meeting, the two sides announced a [working group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_group "Working group") on commercial issues and an export control enforcement "information exchange" dialogue.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-133) During an October 2023 trip to Abu Dhabi, she raised concerns about [G42](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G42_(company) "G42 (company)")'s ties to China.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-nyt202311-134)

On March 11, 2024, on the United States Presidential Trade Mission to the Philippines, Raimondo met [Alfredo E. Pascual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfredo_E._Pascual "Alfredo E. Pascual") and Assistant to the President for Investment and Economic Affairs Frederick Go at [Solaire Resort & Casino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solaire_Resort_&_Casino "Solaire Resort & Casino") and said, "On this trip alone, these 22 company heads in the delegation are announcing over $1 billion of U.S. investments, including educational [and training] opportunities to over 30 million Filipinos in the form of digital upskilling, artificial intelligence upskilling, and digital training."[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-135)

#### Response to port strike

On October 1, 2024, the [International Longshoremen's Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Longshoremen's_Association "International Longshoremen's Association") struck 37 ports in the eastern and south central U.S., curtailing import and export activity between the U.S. and its trade partners. Raimondo was criticized for an interview the previous day on CNBC's *[Squawk Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squawk_Box "Squawk Box")* in which she acknowledged that the strike "could be very disruptive to commerce" but said she was not focused on the issue and "not particularly involved", referring questions to the White House and Transportation Secretary.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-136)

## Post-Biden administration

In January 2025, Raimondo joined the [Council on Foreign Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_Foreign_Relations "Council on Foreign Relations") as a distinguished fellow.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-auto-137) In April 2025, Raimondo joined the advisory board for Bloomberg New Economy as its chair.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-138)

In November of 2025, Raimondo was appointed Co-Chair of [New Jersey Governor-elect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_Jersey "Governor of New Jersey") [Mikie Sherrill’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikie_Sherrill "Mikie Sherrill") “Driving New Jersey Forward: Economic Development and Innovation” committee.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-auto-137)

In 2026, Raimondo became the CEO of [RAISE US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAISE_US "RAISE US"), a non-profit organization which aims to address the disruption to American workers caused by artificial intelligence.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-139). The non-profit is backed, and largely funded, by prominent members of big tech such as Anthropic, Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI, and has prominently spoken out against the idea of universal basic income as a solution to AI-driven job loss, preferring to fund retraining programs.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-140). Raimondo has said previously, prior to becoming CEO of RAISE US, that past federal efforts focused on retraining in response to job loss were ineffective.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-141).

## Personal life and recognition

On December 1, 2001, Raimondo married Andrew Kind Moffit, in Providence.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-148) The couple have two children. The family resides on the east side of Providence. Raimondo is a practicing Catholic and was one of the first girls to graduate from the [La Salle Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Salle_Academy_(Rhode_Island) "La Salle Academy (Rhode Island)"), a Catholic school in Providence.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-149)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-Tom_Mooney-23)

Raimondo is a member of the [Council on Foreign Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_Foreign_Relations "Council on Foreign Relations") (CFR) and an [Aspen Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspen_Institute "Aspen Institute") Rodel fellow. She was awarded an [honorary degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_degree "Honorary degree") from [Bryant University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryant_University "Bryant University") in 2012 and has received awards from the northern Rhode Island [chamber of commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_of_commerce "Chamber of commerce") and the [YWCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YWCA "YWCA") of northern Rhode Island. Raimondo was elected alumni fellow of Yale in 2014.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-150)

On January 27, 2025, CFR announced that Raimondo will join the Council as a DC-based distinguished fellow, co-chairing its Task Force on economic security.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-151)

### Community service

Raimondo serves as vice chair of the board of directors of Crossroads Rhode Island, the state's largest homeless services organization. Until 2011, she was an administrator of [Women and Infants Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_&_Infants_Hospital_of_Rhode_Island "Women & Infants Hospital of Rhode Island") and chair of its Quality Committee. She has served on the boards of La Salle Academy and Family Service of Rhode Island.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo#cite_note-152)
